Elections roadshow: Communities stepping up in the Eastern Cape

By: Laura Byrne | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Eastern Cape is South Africa's poorest province, dogged by poverty, poor service provision and lack of development...but some communities are creating solutions to these problems for themselves.

Unique Selling Point:
Anyone looking at the political landscape in the years running up to 1994 may understandably have believed that the Eastern Cape would have a bright and favoured future in the era of democracy. The ANC’s birthplace, it was home to many of the independence movement’s brightest stars, and its vast area offers international ports, established industry and large-scale farming. However, today the Eastern Cape is South Africa’s poorest province and in many ways the quality of life for people living there has declined since the advent of democracy. There is an ongoing exodus of the youth and skilled workers who see no future for themselves in their own birthplaces. Much of the population is rural, dependent on subsistence farming and migrant labour. Services in many areas are non-existent: children walk many kilometres to reach schools that are often without teachers or even formal buildings. Many villagers die in their own homes from preventable conditions, unable to reach local clinics that themselves may be without supplies or medical staff. Of its 39 municipalities, 11 are considered dysfunctional, 14 medium risk, 14 low risk and none of them stable, according to an August 2021 report prepared for parliament’s portfolio committee on Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs.
We are used to hearing about the decay of infrastructure, the stagnation of innovation, the grind of daily survival. Community projects, when they get attention, are often run by relative outsiders – white doctors at the district hospital, or expats running the local backpackers. Our story will take cognisance of all that, but recognise where people are taking matters into their own hands and creating services for themselves that their government is failing to provide for them.

Summary:
CASE STUDY 1: ZENZELENI COOPERATIVE
We visit Mankozi, where the community has run its own affordable Wi-Fi network since 2012. The Zenzeleni (“Do it yourself”) network has grown from a wireless intranet on analogue phones to a fully licensed internet service provider connected through fibre. It has connected Mankozi to Mthatha and in 2018 expanded to a second cooperative ISP in Zithulele, 56km away.
THEMES: Local economic development, and a side-step into education (usually a provincial mandate): local pupils use the network to apply for tertiary education grants and [hopefully] learn under lockdown.

CASE STUDY 2: NGQUTHU CLINIC
Ngquthu is a village of about 800 people with almost no road access to neighbouring centres. The nearest clinic is at Nqabarah, 8km away across a river that floods in summer – it serves 32 villages and closes in the afternoon. Several women have been raped as they make the 2-hour walk. A mobile clinic that used to visit the village stopped coming years ago. So the community pulled together, donating money towards zinc sheets, and building a clinic. But despite begging government to help them staff and supply the building, healthcare is still unavailable.
THEMES: Infrastructure, access to basic healthcare and community safety.

CASE STUDY 3: CLEAN QUEENSTOWN
The Enoch Mgijima Local Municipality (Queenstown) is tied for last place in the latest Ratings Afrika Index. The municipality is bankrupt, service delivery is nonexistent…residents have had enough. Sean Russell, director of the local funeral parlour, invests his own funds and donations to clear drains and pavements, repair and repaint bridge railings, and install rubbish bins. Two other locals started a similar campaign, Clean Queenstown, in July 2021.
THEMES: Service delivery, infrastructure, economic opportunity.

Further information:
The Eastern Cape is one of South Africa’s poorest provinces, incorporating large areas of the former homelands. It has the highest unemployment rate in the country.
93.1% do not complete their secondary education;
50% do not have access to early education programmes
73.1% have no formal sanitation services;
16.6% live without any form of income;
38.3% of the economically active population is unemployed.

According to COGTA’s annual report for 2019-2020, a recent Stats SA report revealed that the Eastern Cape has the highest rate of “skip generation” households (where grandparents care for grandchildren) in the country, at 8.5%. The same survey showed that the greatest improvement to water access, improved sanitation and electricity between 2002 and 2018 took place in the Eastern Cape. In many areas, people remain dependent on subsistence farming. The province has 13.5% of SA’s population (at almost 7 million) but contributes only 8% of national GDP.

Municipalities (metropolitan, district and local) are responsible for growing local economies and providing infrastructure and services. Metropolitan councils may decentralise their powers and responsibilities, although they retain ultimate legislative and executive power. District councils are largely responsible for capacity-building and planning, including monitoring performance, preparing budgets, decision-making about provision of services for local municipalities.
The five focus areas of the Local Government Turnaround Strategy are service delivery, governance, financial management, infrastructure development, and fighting corruption.
A Municipal Infrastructure Grant, aimed at ensuring basic service provision including water, sanitation, roads, and lighting. There is also a Community Work Programme aimed at providing employment opportunities, with a R13 billion budget between 2018 and 2022.
The Local Economic Development programme is intended to allow local communities to work together to create sustainable economic growth, employment and development.

ZENZELENI
Mankozi is in Nyandeni Municipality, one of five making up the OR Tambo District Municipality. It is largely rural and traditional settlement, with 64.6% living in traditional dwellings, and dependent on agriculture. In 2011, the population was 290 390 people, 99.4% black. Those aged 14 and under made up 40.6% of the population. Only 4.2% of the population had a higher qualification and 18.2% had no form of education.
In 2011, 55.3% of the population had no access to piped water and 33.4% had no access to sanitation. 71% had access to electricity for lighting. Only 1.8% of households had formal refuse removal; 68.3% used their own refuse dumps and 25.5% had no rubbish removal at all.
In 2011, the unemployment rate stood at 44.8%. 80% of households had a cellphone, but 83.1% had no access to internet at all, and only 1.3% had access from home.
According to COGTA’s annual report for 2019-2020, a recent Stats SA survey showed that the Eastern Cape (7.6%) and Northern Cape were the two provinces in which the highest number of households did not have access to communication media in 2018. The national proportion was 3.4%. The Eastern Cape was also one of two provinces (with Limpopo at 46.2%) where the highest proportion of households did not have any access to the internet (55.3%). Only 10.4% of all South Africans had access to the internet at home.

NGQUTHU
Ngquthu is in the Mbhashe local municipality (established 2000), within the Amathole District Municipality. According to Stats SA, Mbhashe had a population in 2011 of 254 909, of which 99.4% were black and 0.2% were white. 38% of the population was aged 14 and younger. Tribal or traditional settlements were most common at 93.7% of the area, with urban areas at 6.3%. Most households were agricultural. The unemployment rate is listed at 42.4% and 14% of households listed no income. Over 60% of households listed an average income of under R40k. Of those aged 20 and older, 21.2% had no form of schooling. Only 5.1% had higher education. Notably, many of these statistics had barely shifted since the previous census in 2001.
Of the 60 000 plus households, 49.7% had access to electricity and only 3.5% had access to piped water indoors. Very few households (3.1%) had regular, municipal or private refuse removal: the majority had their own refuse dump or no refuse disposal. However, according to the Municipality's Integrated Development Plan for 2017-2022,
“Waste Management Services is the main municipal service rendered by Mbhashe” and by 2017, all households had rural waste management. Goals for the next five years included licensing and upgrades to landfill sites, closure and rehabilitation of illegal landfills, and waste awareness and bylaws.
The IDP also notes that the municipality has a huge backlog in roads (80% of municipal roads). A Roads Forum was established in 2012, attended by intersectional departments including Health and Education. The municipality had also purchased “road machines” and started a maintenance schedule. According to the IDP, Mbhashe “relies entirely on Grant to deliver services to its communities. This means the approximately R60 million mentioned above, which is the municipality’s Municipal Infrastructure Grant, is the total income with which the municipality maintains and builds roads - although there was an in-kind investment of R70 million by the province.
Mbhashe is also implementing two household electrification projects. There were protests in 2014-2016 for priority in electrification, in response to which the municipality took a loan from the Department of Energy to speed up the process. At the time of publication there remained 25 375 households with “backlogs” and the electrification plan indicated that some of those would not be provided even within the next three years, and there was a plan to provide those villages with solar panels instead.
The IDP stipulates “Mbhashe Municipality is responsible for community street lighting to ensure safety to communities” - it was aiming to install lighting separate from Eskom infrastructure,and accordingly installed 6 high masts in beach and township areas. However, 4 had to be removed and 2 modified due to environmental issues.
HEALTH SERVICES IN MBHASHE: According to the IDP, at time of publication there were 29 residential clinics, 3 community health centres, one district hospital, six mobile clinics and seven functional health posts in the municipality. In 2014/2015, Mbhashe was awarded best-performing sub district in HIV/AIDS, TB and mother, child and women’s health programmes, in the Amathole District Awards. However, the IDP notes ongoing issues including HIV and ART use (23.2% defaulting), teenage pregnancy, TB management and screening, malnutrition, waterborne diseases, family planning, antenatal care and infection control.
Other responsibilities of the municipality include provision of destitute housing, early childhood development centres, community halls, cemeteries, sports fields, ablutions, maintenance of beaches. The budget “is very limited and does not cover all the capital and operating expenses of the municipality”. Income is from grants, and rates and services. The municipality is only collecting 32% of budgeted revenue at R251 million. Total revenue in 2015/2016 was R313 967 402 of which R290 million came from grants and subsidies. Its expenditure in the same year was R267 504 427, of which the biggest chunk was personnel costs. The municipality spent 100% of all its grants, and overspent the MIG by almost R16 million. A large proportion of their equitable share income seems to be going towards corporate services, in other words training, facilities etc for the municipal employees. Much less was aimed towards KPA2: service delivery.
Burgling of clinics, inconsistent/nonexistent electricity supply, poor roads, personnel retention, poor transport, lack of communication infrastructure, lack of water and sanitation are all issues affecting healthcare.

QUEENSTOWN
The Enoch Mgijima Local Municipality (often referred to as Queenstown) is tied for last place in the latest Ratings Afrika Municipal Financial Stability Index, with a score of just 9 out of 100. Carte Blanche ran a story in 2018 about the municipality’s auction of its vehicles and planned auction of some buildings to pay off a historical construction debt. [MORE INFO COMING HERE]
Local businesses donate meals, materials and tools towards the clean-up efforts, and they post daily about their activities on Facebook, often tagging the local municipality in an attempt to ‘inspire’ them.

Press Release:


Vuka Uzenzele Eastern Cape
The breath taking vistas, rich historical legacy and distinct culture of the Eastern Cape – the birthplace of so many South African leadership icons – belie an ongoing tragedy of underdevelopment and municipal mismanagement. Divided into six district and two metropolitan municipalities, not one of these have been declared stable or functional by the Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs in its last report. Growth in the province remains chronically stunted and most communities fail to receive the most basic services. So what will shape residents’ actions in the coming local election? Carte Blanche investigates how from Mankozi to Ngquthu villagers are taking back control and finding their own solutions to decades-long problems.


Script:


VO: It’s morning in Mlungisi township, eKomani - formerly Queenstown. Simamnkele Vanqa and Simon Mphele are preparing for their day’s work as the town’s self-appointed maintenance men. Sponsored by local businesses, they clear litter and repaint landmarks like this bridge.

UPSOUND: SIMON AND SIMA: 00:12:58 We chose this bridge because it's like an entrance point in Queenstown, So it's like it gives you the first impression of your town, right?

VO: Enoch Mgijima Local Municipality has the dubious distinction of being tied for last place in the latest Ratings Afrika Municipal Financial Stability Index. Evidence of the decay is everywhere.

LINK: Recently, the municipality faced social media outrage after announcing the opening of this sports facility - really no more than a fenced field - at a hefty R15 million. Unfortunately, this is just the latest example of municipal mismanagement in the Eastern Cape.

VO: The municipality responded on social media, saying the scope of work is greater than first reported.

LINK: But some parts of Komani are showing a little life again, thanks to a few passionate locals.

UPSOUND: SIMA: The environment sets the moods, like people's moods. So if you got a foul environment, you're going to be in a foul mood, whereas cleanliness always makes people feel happy, you know.

UPSOUND: SIMON: 03:07 So instead of pointing fingers, we're like no, we can tackle this, we can do it ourselves.

VO: It was another staunch Komani citizen who inspired all this positive activity. Sean Russell is director of a local funeral parlour, which marks its centenary this year.

UPSOUND SEAN RUSSELL: I said to my team, I'm not going to be spending money on frivolous parties and nonsense and how would they feel about it if I bought this machine, I bought a tractor, I bought a trailer with community support and I'll start cleaning the town. The problem is that this kind of mess, as you can see, has not been around for a week or two. This is 10, 15 years of no cleaning.

VO: Russell has spent 18 months cleaning parks, cutting grass, and repainting road markings.

UPSOUND: SEAN RUSSELL: I really enjoy the fact the community's involvement. Some of the lows is... clean up an area and you come back a week later and it's all dirty again. But that to me, is just indicative of the fact that there is no plan in place to help or accommodate the community and stop them from drowning in refuse.

VO: Local government is in crisis across South Africa. According to a recent report by the Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs, a quarter of our municipalities are dysfunctional. Only five and a half percent are stable - not one of which can be found in the Eastern Cape.

LINK: Waste management is one of the primary responsibilities of local government - along with infrastructure and economic development. A failure at this level has huge consequences.

VO: Like here in Ngquthu, in Mbhashe Local Municipality, 200km east of eKomani. It’s 3PM and these women are starting the two-hour walk from Nqabara Clinic, which serves 32 surrounding villages. They’ve been here since 8AM. It’s a dangerous journey: several women have been raped on their way to or from Nqabara. This woman is one of them.

UPSOUND: RAPE VICTIM: He said if you don’t want to give me the phone I will kill you. He wanted to drown me. I thought I could fight back, but because he wanted to stab me in my chest, I couldn’t. Now, I’m unable to walk alone. I always think back to that road I was walking on.

VO: But the villagers have no alternative route. Ngquthu has no clinic of its own and the mobile clinic has visited just twice this year. Sinazo Shumi is head of the village council.

UPSOUND SINAZO SHUMI: The last time the nurses came here was when they came to vaccinate the elderly for COVID-19- that was the 19th of July. A lot of people here have high blood pressure, they have asthma, so they can't travel that long distance.

VO: The Municipality’s Integrated Development Plan lists poor road networks as one of many issues affecting healthcare - and it’s easy to see why. For these villagers, the state of the roads can literally be a matter of life and death.

UPSOUND SINAZO: The ambulances cannot come in because we don’t have a road. If you call an ambulance you have to meet it halfway.

VO: So with the little they had, the villagers refurbished a disused preschool into their own makeshift clinic.

UPSOUND:SINAZO: People could say this is just a shack, but to us this is something huge. Our elders decided to collect money. They depend on social grants…so they decided each household should contribute R100.

VO: But without further resources the clinic is just an empty shell.

UPSOUND: SINAZO: The main reason we can't finish this is because there aren’t many of us, we can't ask them to contribute again, the government should come in and help where they come short. We ask government to provide pills for them in this shack so that they can receive their treatment here. We don’t know if someone will eventually die.

VO: The Eastern Cape Department of Health did not respond to our request for comment in time for broadcast.
Life in Ngquthu is hard: even fetching water means walking for hours. The Mbashe Local Municipality Is not a Water Service Provider and relies on the Amathole District Municipality for water services. Shumi says Amathole installed taps like this one back in 2013, but not a single drop has ever come from them. So along with 56% of Mbhashe’s rural population, these villagers are reliant on rainwater tanks and rivers.

UPSOUND: SINAZO: We get water down there and through the forest there, older people can't get there, the water is filthy, we drink with cows.

VO: Amathole District Municipality says the taps are part of a water provision project awaiting funding for its next phase.

UPSOUND: SINAZO: We have been forgotten, I don’t want to hide that.

VO: 150km away, the sun is setting over Mankozi in Nyandeni Local Municipality. It’s a rustic setting - but atop this hill is an unexpected sight: a brand new, solar powered computer lab.

UPSOUND: YUMNA PANDAY: It's connectivity, affordable connectivity and creating or being part of creating a digital ecosystem. Everybody knows about the internet, but they don't know what the internet, information, can do for them.

VO: This is Yumna Panday, and the internet she’s talking about is Zenzeleni, a community-owned network that supplies affordable wifi to this remote spot. Fifty five percent of Eastern Cape households have no internet access at all. As services like school registration increasingly go online, they are closed out of the loop.

UPSOUND: JAY SIYA: So you are kind of making everyone to be more equal in terms of having access to the services.

VO: Zenzeleni is the brainchild of Mankozi-born Masbulele Jay Siya. It connects over 80 community hotspots, where villagers pay just R25 for a month’s uncapped internet.

UPSOUND: JAY: You can study, do payments, can run the business. And we in the Wild Coast, you know. So then if we have internet, the tourism itself is kind of growing.

UPSOUND: YUMNA: People are now connecting to the network for information to actually find out what's going on. The content that was pushed initially was basically, you know, social media, YouTube. Now people are Googling more.

UPSOUND: MIHLALI TYILO: I use it if I need to access like patient care results, because most of your decisions that you make depend on those lab results.

VO: Zenzeleni also provides low-cost wifi to Zithulele District Hospital. Dr Mihlali Tyilo is seeing the benefits.

UPSOUND: MIHLALI: I also use it to access medical apps. And that's quite helpful because I don't carry around like medical textbooks with me. So everything I need I can access on my smartphone.

UPSOUND: KARL LE ROUX: The ability to access good resources in terms of health care has made a massive difference to our clinical team, meaning that we can really, really kind of give people the best care they can possibly get in the time that we have available.

VO: Dr Karl le Roux has lived and worked in this community for 15 years.

UPSOUND: KARL: And I think the other thing is just actually for the hospital staff, to have a good internet connection makes people feel closer to their family who might be in the cities, and it means that retaining and keeping people in this rural area is a lot easier than it was maybe five years ago.

VO: The network has now expanded to Zithulele village, where chief Avuyile Dudumayo is enthusiastic about its potential to uplift the community.

UPSOUND: CHIEF DUDUMAYO: We try to engage with government, sometimes they do come to the fore but there is little money allocated by the local municipality. It's depressing that there are people who are supposed to do their job, but the community has to try and do it on their own.

VO: Doing it yourself comes at a price. Eighty percent of the cost of one of these towers is back-up power to bolster the municipality’s unreliable supply.

LINK: These communities are applying all the resources they have to create solutions for themselves. The problem is, infrastructure and bulk services require big money and organising power - in other words, government needs to come to the party.

UPSOUND: SINAZO: Our parents have been voting, their IDs are full of voting stamps and we don’t see progress, we don't see anything happening.

UPSOUND SEAN: I'm one of those ever optimists. that believes some point somewhere that municipality will pull itself together. Are they coming to find a town totally destroyed or are they going to find a town that is semi floating, so that when they do come back, they have got something to just take on and carry on.

PROMO
UPSOUND: SINAZO: The ambulances cannot come in because we don’t have a road. If you call an ambulance you have to meet it halfway.
VO: We are in the Eastern Cape, where municipal mismanagement and decay is chronic. We visit communities battling to undo decades-long dysfunction and neglect.
UPSOUND: SEAN RUSSELL: This kind of mess, as you can see, has not been around for a week or two. This is 10,15 years of no cleaning.

In 2011, 55.3% of the population had no access to piped water and 33.4% had no access to sanitation. 71% had access to electricity for lighting. Only 1.8% of households had formal refuse removal; 68.3% used their own refuse dumps and 25.5% had no rubbish removal at all. In 2011, the unemployment rate stood at 44.8%. 80% of households had a cellphone, but 83.1% had no access to internet at all, and only 1.3% had access from home. According to COGTA’s annual report for 2019-2020, a recent Stats SA survey showed that the Eastern Cape (7.6%) and Northern Cape were the two provinces in which the highest number of households did not have access to communication media in 2018. The national proportion was 3.4%. The Eastern Cape was also one of two provinces (with Limpopo at 46.2%) where the highest proportion of households did not have any access to the internet (55.3%). Only 10.4% of all South Africans had access to the internet at home. NGQUTHU Ngquthu is in the Mbhashe local municipality (established 2000), within the Amathole District Municipality. According to Stats SA, Mbhashe had a population in 2011 of 254 909, of which 99.4% were black and 0.2% were white. 38% of the population was aged 14 and younger. Tribal or traditional settlements were most common at 93.7% of the area, with urban areas at 6.3%. Most households were agricultural. The unemployment rate is listed at 42.4% and 14% of households listed no income. Over 60% of households listed an average income of under R40k. Of those aged 20 and older, 21.2% had no form of schooling. Only 5.1% had higher education. Notably, many of these statistics had barely shifted since the previous census in 2001. Of the 60 000 plus households, 49.7% had access to electricity and only 3.5% had access to piped water indoors. Very few households (3.1%) had regular, municipal or private refuse removal: the majority had their own refuse dump or no refuse disposal. However, according to the Municipality's Integrated Development Plan for 2017-2022, “Waste Management Services is the main municipal service rendered by Mbhashe” and by 2017, all households had rural waste management. Goals for the next five years included licensing and upgrades to landfill sites, closure and rehabilitation of illegal landfills, and waste awareness and bylaws. The IDP also notes that the municipality has a huge backlog in roads (80% of municipal roads). A Roads Forum was established in 2012, attended by intersectional departments including Health and Education. The municipality had also purchased “road machines” and started a maintenance schedule. According to the IDP, Mbhashe “relies entirely on Grant to deliver services to its communities. This means the approximately R60 million mentioned above, which is the municipality’s Municipal Infrastructure Grant, is the total income with which the municipality maintains and builds roads - although there was an in-kind investment of R70 million by the province. Mbhashe is also implementing two household electrification projects. There were protests in 2014-2016 for priority in electrification, in response to which the municipality took a loan from the Department of Energy to speed up the process. At the time of publication there remained 25 375 households with “backlogs” and the electrification plan indicated that some of those would not be provided even within the next three years, and there was a plan to provide those villages with solar panels instead. The IDP stipulates “Mbhashe Municipality is responsible for community street lighting to ensure safety to communities” - it was aiming to install lighting separate from Eskom infrastructure,and accordingly installed 6 high masts in beach and township areas. However, 4 had to be removed and 2 modified due to environmental issues. HEALTH SERVICES IN MBHASHE: According to the IDP, at time of publication there were 29 residential clinics, 3 community health centres, one district hospital, six mobile clinics and seven functional health posts in the municipality. In 2014/2015, Mbhashe was awarded best-performing sub district in HIV/AIDS, TB and mother, child and women’s health programmes, in the Amathole District Awards. However, the IDP notes ongoing issues including HIV and ART use (23.2% defaulting), teenage pregnancy, TB management and screening, malnutrition, waterborne diseases, family planning, antenatal care and infection control. Other responsibilities of the municipality include provision of destitute housing, early childhood development centres, community halls, cemeteries, sports fields, ablutions, maintenance of beaches. The budget “is very limited and does not cover all the capital and operating expenses of the municipality”. Income is from grants, and rates and services. The municipality is only collecting 32% of budgeted revenue at R251 million. Total revenue in 2015/2016 was R313 967 402 of which R290 million came from grants and subsidies. Its expenditure in the same year was R267 504 427, of which the biggest chunk was personnel costs. The municipality spent 100% of all its grants, and overspent the MIG by almost R16 million. A large proportion of their equitable share income seems to be going towards corporate services, in other words training, facilities etc for the municipal employees. Much less was aimed towards KPA2: service delivery. Burgling of clinics, inconsistent/nonexistent electricity supply, poor roads, personnel retention, poor transport, lack of communication infrastructure, lack of water and sanitation are all issues affecting healthcare. QUEENSTOWN The Enoch Mgijima Local Municipality (often referred to as Queenstown) is tied for last place in the latest Ratings Afrika Municipal Financial Stability Index, with a score of just 9 out of 100. Carte Blanche ran a story in 2018 about the municipality’s auction of its vehicles and planned auction of some buildings to pay off a historical construction debt. [MORE INFO COMING HERE] Local businesses donate meals, materials and tools towards the clean-up efforts, and they post daily about their activities on Facebook, often tagging the local municipality in an attempt to ‘inspire’ them. Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 17 October 2021 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 07 November 2021 Press Release: Vuka Uzenzele Eastern Cape The breath taking vistas, rich historical legacy and distinct culture of the Eastern Cape – the birthplace of so many South African leadership icons – belie an ongoing tragedy of underdevelopment and municipal mismanagement. Divided into six district and two metropolitan municipalities, not one of these have been declared stable or functional by the Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs in its last report. Growth in the province remains chronically stunted and most communities fail to receive the most basic services. So what will shape residents’ actions in the coming local election? Carte Blanche investigates how from Mankozi to Ngquthu villagers are taking back control and finding their own solutions to decades-long problems. Script: VO: It’s morning in Mlungisi township, eKomani - formerly Queenstown. Simamnkele Vanqa and Simon Mphele are preparing for their day’s work as the town’s self-appointed maintenance men. Sponsored by local businesses, they clear litter and repaint landmarks like this bridge. UPSOUND: SIMON AND SIMA: 00:12:58 We chose this bridge because it's like an entrance point in Queenstown, So it's like it gives you the first impression of your town, right? VO: Enoch Mgijima Local Municipality has the dubious distinction of being tied for last place in the latest Ratings Afrika Municipal Financial Stability Index. Evidence of the decay is everywhere. LINK: Recently, the municipality faced social media outrage after announcing the opening of this sports facility - really no more than a fenced field - at a hefty R15 million. Unfortunately, this is just the latest example of municipal mismanagement in the Eastern Cape. VO: The municipality responded on social media, saying the scope of work is greater than first reported. LINK: But some parts of Komani are showing a little life again, thanks to a few passionate locals. UPSOUND: SIMA: The environment sets the moods, like people's moods. So if you got a foul environment, you're going to be in a foul mood, whereas cleanliness always makes people feel happy, you know. UPSOUND: SIMON: 03:07 So instead of pointing fingers, we're like no, we can tackle this, we can do it ourselves. VO: It was another staunch Komani citizen who inspired all this positive activity. Sean Russell is director of a local funeral parlour, which marks its centenary this year. UPSOUND SEAN RUSSELL: I said to my team, I'm not going to be spending money on frivolous parties and nonsense and how would they feel about it if I bought this machine, I bought a tractor, I bought a trailer with community support and I'll start cleaning the town. The problem is that this kind of mess, as you can see, has not been around for a week or two. This is 10, 15 years of no cleaning. VO: Russell has spent 18 months cleaning parks, cutting grass, and repainting road markings. UPSOUND: SEAN RUSSELL: I really enjoy the fact the community's involvement. Some of the lows is... clean up an area and you come back a week later and it's all dirty again. But that to me, is just indicative of the fact that there is no plan in place to help or accommodate the community and stop them from drowning in refuse. VO: Local government is in crisis across South Africa. According to a recent report by the Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs, a quarter of our municipalities are dysfunctional. Only five and a half percent are stable - not one of which can be found in the Eastern Cape. LINK: Waste management is one of the primary responsibilities of local government - along with infrastructure and economic development. A failure at this level has huge consequences. VO: Like here in Ngquthu, in Mbhashe Local Municipality, 200km east of eKomani. It’s 3PM and these women are starting the two-hour walk from Nqabara Clinic, which serves 32 surrounding villages. They’ve been here since 8AM. It’s a dangerous journey: several women have been raped on their way to or from Nqabara. This woman is one of them. UPSOUND: RAPE VICTIM: He said if you don’t want to give me the phone I will kill you. He wanted to drown me. I thought I could fight back, but because he wanted to stab me in my chest, I couldn’t. Now, I’m unable to walk alone. I always think back to that road I was walking on. VO: But the villagers have no alternative route. Ngquthu has no clinic of its own and the mobile clinic has visited just twice this year. Sinazo Shumi is head of the village council. UPSOUND SINAZO SHUMI: The last time the nurses came here was when they came to vaccinate the elderly for COVID-19- that was the 19th of July. A lot of people here have high blood pressure, they have asthma, so they can't travel that long distance. VO: The Municipality’s Integrated Development Plan lists poor road networks as one of many issues affecting healthcare - and it’s easy to see why. For these villagers, the state of the roads can literally be a matter of life and death. UPSOUND SINAZO: The ambulances cannot come in because we don’t have a road. If you call an ambulance you have to meet it halfway. VO: So with the little they had, the villagers refurbished a disused preschool into their own makeshift clinic. UPSOUND:SINAZO: People could say this is just a shack, but to us this is something huge. Our elders decided to collect money. They depend on social grants…so they decided each household should contribute R100. VO: But without further resources the clinic is just an empty shell. UPSOUND: SINAZO: The main reason we can't finish this is because there aren’t many of us, we can't ask them to contribute again, the government should come in and help where they come short. We ask government to provide pills for them in this shack so that they can receive their treatment here. We don’t know if someone will eventually die. VO: The Eastern Cape Department of Health did not respond to our request for comment in time for broadcast. Life in Ngquthu is hard: even fetching water means walking for hours. The Mbashe Local Municipality Is not a Water Service Provider and relies on the Amathole District Municipality for water services. Shumi says Amathole installed taps like this one back in 2013, but not a single drop has ever come from them. So along with 56% of Mbhashe’s rural population, these villagers are reliant on rainwater tanks and rivers. UPSOUND: SINAZO: We get water down there and through the forest there, older people can't get there, the water is filthy, we drink with cows. VO: Amathole District Municipality says the taps are part of a water provision project awaiting funding for its next phase. UPSOUND: SINAZO: We have been forgotten, I don’t want to hide that. VO: 150km away, the sun is setting over Mankozi in Nyandeni Local Municipality. It’s a rustic setting - but atop this hill is an unexpected sight: a brand new, solar powered computer lab. UPSOUND: YUMNA PANDAY: It's connectivity, affordable connectivity and creating or being part of creating a digital ecosystem. Everybody knows about the internet, but they don't know what the internet, information, can do for them. VO: This is Yumna Panday, and the internet she’s talking about is Zenzeleni, a community-owned network that supplies affordable wifi to this remote spot. Fifty five percent of Eastern Cape households have no internet access at all. As services like school registration increasingly go online, they are closed out of the loop. UPSOUND: JAY SIYA: So you are kind of making everyone to be more equal in terms of having access to the services. VO: Zenzeleni is the brainchild of Mankozi-born Masbulele Jay Siya. It connects over 80 community hotspots, where villagers pay just R25 for a month’s uncapped internet. UPSOUND: JAY: You can study, do payments, can run the business. And we in the Wild Coast, you know. So then if we have internet, the tourism itself is kind of growing. UPSOUND: YUMNA: People are now connecting to the network for information to actually find out what's going on. The content that was pushed initially was basically, you know, social media, YouTube. Now people are Googling more. UPSOUND: MIHLALI TYILO: I use it if I need to access like patient care results, because most of your decisions that you make depend on those lab results. VO: Zenzeleni also provides low-cost wifi to Zithulele District Hospital. Dr Mihlali Tyilo is seeing the benefits. UPSOUND: MIHLALI: I also use it to access medical apps. And that's quite helpful because I don't carry around like medical textbooks with me. So everything I need I can access on my smartphone. UPSOUND: KARL LE ROUX: The ability to access good resources in terms of health care has made a massive difference to our clinical team, meaning that we can really, really kind of give people the best care they can possibly get in the time that we have available. VO: Dr Karl le Roux has lived and worked in this community for 15 years. UPSOUND: KARL: And I think the other thing is just actually for the hospital staff, to have a good internet connection makes people feel closer to their family who might be in the cities, and it means that retaining and keeping people in this rural area is a lot easier than it was maybe five years ago. VO: The network has now expanded to Zithulele village, where chief Avuyile Dudumayo is enthusiastic about its potential to uplift the community. UPSOUND: CHIEF DUDUMAYO: We try to engage with government, sometimes they do come to the fore but there is little money allocated by the local municipality. It's depressing that there are people who are supposed to do their job, but the community has to try and do it on their own. VO: Doing it yourself comes at a price. Eighty percent of the cost of one of these towers is back-up power to bolster the municipality’s unreliable supply. LINK: These communities are applying all the resources they have to create solutions for themselves. The problem is, infrastructure and bulk services require big money and organising power - in other words, government needs to come to the party. UPSOUND: SINAZO: Our parents have been voting, their IDs are full of voting stamps and we don’t see progress, we don't see anything happening. UPSOUND SEAN: I'm one of those ever optimists. that believes some point somewhere that municipality will pull itself together. Are they coming to find a town totally destroyed or are they going to find a town that is semi floating, so that when they do come back, they have got something to just take on and carry on. PROMO UPSOUND: SINAZO: The ambulances cannot come in because we don’t have a road. If you call an ambulance you have to meet it halfway. VO: We are in the Eastern Cape, where municipal mismanagement and decay is chronic. We visit communities battling to undo decades-long dysfunction and neglect. UPSOUND: SEAN RUSSELL: This kind of mess, as you can see, has not been around for a week or two. This is 10,15 years of no cleaning.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The Eastern Cape is South Africa's poorest province, dogged by poverty, poor service provision and lack of development...but some communities are creating solutions to these problems for themselves.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Anyone looking at the political landscape in the years running up to 1994 may understandably have believed that the Eastern Cape would have a bright and favoured future in the era of democracy. The ANC’s birthplace, it was home to many of the independence movement’s brightest stars, and its vast area offers international ports, established industry and large-scale farming. However, today the Eastern Cape is South Africa’s poorest province and in many ways the quality of life for people living there has declined since the advent of democracy. There is an ongoing exodus of the youth and skilled workers who see no future for themselves in their own birthplaces. Much of the population is rural, dependent on subsistence farming and migrant labour. Services in many areas are non-existent: children walk many kilometres to reach schools that are often without teachers or even formal buildings. Many villagers die in their own homes from preventable conditions, unable to reach local clinics that themselves may be without supplies or medical staff. Of its 39 municipalities, 11 are considered dysfunctional, 14 medium risk, 14 low risk and none of them stable, according to an August 2021 report prepared for parliament’s portfolio committee on Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs. We are used to hearing about the decay of infrastructure, the stagnation of innovation, the grind of daily survival. Community projects, when they get attention, are often run by relative outsiders – white doctors at the district hospital, or expats running the local backpackers. Our story will take cognisance of all that, but recognise where people are taking matters into their own hands and creating services for themselves that their government is failing to provide for them.
metadata.Summary: CASE STUDY 1: ZENZELENI COOPERATIVE We visit Mankozi, where the community has run its own affordable Wi-Fi network since 2012. The Zenzeleni (“Do it yourself”) network has grown from a wireless intranet on analogue phones to a fully licensed internet service provider connected through fibre. It has connected Mankozi to Mthatha and in 2018 expanded to a second cooperative ISP in Zithulele, 56km away. THEMES: Local economic development, and a side-step into education (usually a provincial mandate): local pupils use the network to apply for tertiary education grants and [hopefully] learn under lockdown. CASE STUDY 2: NGQUTHU CLINIC Ngquthu is a village of about 800 people with almost no road access to neighbouring centres. The nearest clinic is at Nqabarah, 8km away across a river that floods in summer – it serves 32 villages and closes in the afternoon. Several women have been raped as they make the 2-hour walk. A mobile clinic that used to visit the village stopped coming years ago. So the community pulled together, donating money towards zinc sheets, and building a clinic. But despite begging government to help them staff and supply the building, healthcare is still unavailable. THEMES: Infrastructure, access to basic healthcare and community safety. CASE STUDY 3: CLEAN QUEENSTOWN The Enoch Mgijima Local Municipality (Queenstown) is tied for last place in the latest Ratings Afrika Index. The municipality is bankrupt, service delivery is nonexistent…residents have had enough. Sean Russell, director of the local funeral parlour, invests his own funds and donations to clear drains and pavements, repair and repaint bridge railings, and install rubbish bins. Two other locals started a similar campaign, Clean Queenstown, in July 2021. THEMES: Service delivery, infrastructure, economic opportunity.
